metadata.title: Braised Macomber Turnip (or Rutabaga)
metadata.description:
Recipe and more info:
http://www.beyondsalmon.com/2015/01/braised-macomber-turnip-or-rutabaga.html

Little did I know when making this video that Macomber Turnip is our local legendary Massachusetts treasure (here is the legend).  There is a Russian folk tale about a turnip that grew so big it took a whole family to pull it out of the ground, and being Russian I have a soft spot for big turnips.  If you can't find Macomber Turnips, use any type of Rutabaga.

For Braising:
1 Large Macomber Turnip or Rutabaga
3 Tbsp olive oil
3 Tbsp madeira, white wine, chicken stock, or water

Pureeing after Braising:
2 cups braised turnips
3/4 cup milk
1 Tbsp butter

The video shows a woman in a kitchen, making some turnip cakes. She cuts up a turnip. He then cooks it with butter, olive oil, and other seasonings in the pan and then blends it with other ingredients. She then serves it on a dish.
The woman wears a green t-shirt with a silver necklace and stands in a room with white kitchen cabinets. The room has many white plates, bowls and jars on the cabinet. She has short brown hair. She is cooking in a frying pan with olive oil, and she uses a kitchen tong. The tablecloth on which she serves the food is patterned in orange, red and light blue.
The camera is handheld and shaky, but it captures the process of the woman making turnip cakes and serving it on a dish.

summary.brief: A woman prepares, braises, purées, and plates a turnip dish.
summary.detailed: The video follows a woman with short brown hair wearing a green T‑shirt as she makes a braised turnip puree. She begins by peeling a large turnip, then cuts it into thick planks, sticks and finally small dice. The dice are placed in a hot skillet with three tablespoons of olive oil, seasoned with a few pinches of salt, and sautéed while being tossed with kitchen tongs until the pieces turn golden‑brown. After the turnips are browned, she deglazes the pan with about three tablespoons of Madeira (or another liquid) and lets the glaze reduce. The cooked turnip pieces are transferred to a blender where she adds roughly three‑quarters of a cup of milk and a tablespoon of butter, then blends until the mixture is smooth and creamy. She tastes, adjusts the seasoning, and pours the warm puree onto a white plate set on a patterned orange‑red‑blue tablecloth, presenting the finished dish before ending the segment.

action.detailed: Peel the turnip, cut it into dice, sauté the pieces in olive oil with salt using tongs until browned, deglaze the pan with Madeira, blend the cooked turnip with milk and butter until smooth, and plate the puree for serving.
action.actor: a woman wearing a green T‑shirt with short brown hair

The video is a step-by-step tutorial for how to cook a potato and wine dish. A woman stands in a kitchen, explaining the steps as she cuts the potatoes and cooks them. The video is divided into two sections: the first two minutes feature a woman speaking to the camera, the remaining five minutes feature a cooking segment.
The first two minutes feature a woman speaking directly to the camera. She wears an apron and is in the kitchen. The background is a white cabinet and countertop. The woman wears a teal shirt.
The final five minutes are dedicated to a cooking demonstration. First, a white male hands down a knife to a pair of white hands, who chop two potatoes on a wooden cutting board. The potatoes are cut into cubes and then placed in a silver wok. The pot is filled with oil and the potatoes are mixed with more oil and stirred. Once the potatoes are browned, the lid is placed on the pot and the heat is turned down to medium low. The video cuts to a shot of potatoes, which are being stirred inside a pot with a red lid. The potatoes are browned, then a bottle of wine is poured on the potatoes and stirred with a wooden spoon.

The lighting is bright and neutral, with the primary source being the kitchen overhead light. There is natural light entering the scene through an open window. The camera is handheld and stable throughout.

summary.brief: The presenter peels, dices, browns, and braises a large turnip in olive oil and Madeira.
summary.detailed: The video opens with the presenter holding a large turnip and using a vegetable peeler to remove its skin. She cuts off one side to create a flat base, then slices the turnip into thick planks, cuts those into sticks, and finally dices them into uniform cubes. A large skillet is heated over high heat, three tablespoons of olive oil are added until the oil shimmers, and the diced turnip pieces are tossed in, seasoned with a few pinches of salt and coated with oil. After an initial stir, she stops stirring so the pieces can develop a deep brown crust, covering the pan briefly and uncovering it to brown all sides. The heat is then reduced to medium‑low and the pan is kept covered, with occasional stirring every few minutes, until the turnip becomes soft after about 15–20 minutes total. She deglazes the pan by adding roughly three tablespoons of medium‑dry Madeira (or an alternative liquid such as white wine, stock, or water), scraping up the browned bits and allowing the liquid to reduce. Finally she tastes for salt, adjusts seasoning, and notes that the braised turnip can be served as is or pureed with milk and butter.

action.detailed: Peel the turnip, cut it into dice, sauté the dice in hot olive oil until browned, then simmer them with Madeira over medium‑low heat until tender, scraping up the browned bits before finishing.

If you can't find Macomber Turnips, use any type of Rutabaga.

3 Tbsp olive oil
3 Tbsp madeira, white wine, chicken stock, or water

Pureeing after Br
summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video follows a woman with short brown hair wearing a green T‑shirt as she makes a braised turnip puree. She begins by peeling a large turnip, then cuts it into thick planks, sticks and finally small dice. The dice are placed in a hot skillet with three tablespoons of olive oil, seasoned with a few pinches of salt, and sautéed while being tossed with kitchen tongs until the pieces turn golden‑brown. After the turnips are browned, she deglazes the pan with about three tablespoons of Madeira (or another liquid) and lets the glaze reduce. The cooked turnip pieces are transferred to a blender where she adds roughly three‑quarters of a cup of milk and a tablespoon of butter, then blends until the mixture is smooth and creamy. She tastes, adjusts the seasoning, and pours the warm puree onto a white plate set on a patterned orange‑red‑blue tablecloth, presenting the finished dish before ending the segment.
